audit.reasoning: Quote check passes: every fragment of the deciding quotation is verbatim in the held Hartell scanned sheet, the Bird arXiv preprint text (lines 283-382, pp. 6-8) and the Wikipedia raw dump. The 'tonal' classification is safe -- Anufɔ is a Central Tano (Bia) language, Bird's Roberts data show lexical H/L melodies with spread and downstep, Hartell's sheet lists two tones, and the newly downloaded Tasson 2022 (p. 273) gives an H/L minimal triplet kéré/kèré/kèrè and calls Anufo 'a tone language'; no reached source mentions stress. But the record rests on an orthography sheet, a handbook worked example and Wikipedia, while a dedicated phonology (Holman, Holman & Adjekum 1993), a reference grammar (Smye 2004) and SIL phonology field reports (Stanford & Stanford 1970) exist and are unheld and print/lending-only. sources.citation: Tasson, Solomon Kofi. 2022. An analysis in assessing the categories of words borrowed into Anufo. European Journal of Education Studies 9(1): 265-280. DOI 10.46827/ejes.v9i1.4123
sources.quote: 'Anufo as Akan, is a tone language which means that the meaning of a word depends not only on the vowels and consonant of which the word is made, but also on the relative pitch on which each syllable of the word is pronounced ... the tone marks are (´) for high tone ... and (`) for low tone ... Anufo tones are marked on vowels and syllabic consonants. ... [kéré] 'bottle' ... [kèré] 'hat/cap' ... [kèrè] ... to teach or to show.' Syllable types V, CV, syllabic N. No mention of stress or accent anywhere in the article.
